species.look_here_first: Start with one mature intact spikelet: the LOWER glume is usually about half the length of the UPPER glume (roughly 6–8 mm versus 11–15 mm, awns excluded) and normally has ONE vein. Then check the rooted plant for a persistent perennial tuft with many basal rolled leaves and hairs around the collar. Three awns and purple color confirm neither species by themselves.

species.look_here_first: Start with one mature intact spikelet: LOWER and UPPER glumes are normally similar in length (about 18–25 mm without their terminal awns); the lower glume often shows THREE TO SEVEN veins when backlit. Then check that the plant is a wiry, freely branched ANNUAL without a persistent perennial basal crown. The open panicle and long spreading awns help, but aren't proof on their own.

species.look_here_first: FIRST find a MIDDLE STEM LEAF still attached to an opposite leaf node: each leaf is SIMPLE (one lance-shaped blade), sessile or nearly so, often toothed, rather than three separate leaflets attached to a common leafstalk (B. frondosa). SECOND inspect head: usually 7–8 showy yellow rays about 15–25 mm long and 5–7+ OUTER CALYCULUS green leaflike bractlets, then the INNER overlapping phyllaries. THIRD compare mature fruit with B. cernua: B. laevis outer cypselae 6–8 mm, inner 8–10 mm, margins NOT conspicuously thickened or corky-winged, usually 2–4 barbed awns 3–5 mm long; B. cernua fruits have more conspicuous thickened/winged margins, often shorter awns and smaller rays. Both can have nodding ripe heads. Flower color, 'nodding' or wetland site alone are not enough.
